notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 27, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Ezekiel 27 — The Dirge of Tyre: A Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview

All commentators agree that this chapter is a funeral lament (Hebrew *qinah* metre) over Tyre, picturing the city as a magnificent ship that is ultimately wrecked. Ellicott calls it "The Dirge of Tyre" — a lamentation over its fall, not because the prophet wished it otherwise, but because of the terror and sorrow of the event itself. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

The Expositor's Bible notes that "the fiery indignation of the prophet almost disappears, giving place to the play of poetic fancy and a flow of lyric emotion more perfectly rendered than in any other part of Ezekiel's writings." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

---

### vv. 1–2: The Command to Lament

**v. 1:** "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying…" — Gill notes this continues the same subject: the destruction of Tyre. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 2:** "Now you, son of man, take up a lament for Tyre." — Gill explains that the prophet is to compose an elegy like the *praeficae* (mourning women) did at funerals, saying all they could in praise of the dead while making doleful lamentations. He adds: "it may teach us, that even wicked men are to be pitied, when in distress and calamity." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

---

### v. 3: Tyre's Boast

**"You have said, O Tyre, 'I am perfect in beauty.'"** — Gill says Tyre boasted of her good foundation on a rock, walls and towers, well-arranged streets, goodly houses, and fine harbour. He notes that after Jerusalem's destruction, Tyre assumed her character (cf. Psalm 48:2). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik (Enduring Word) notes Tyre was "a proud city," seeing itself as without limits. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**"Who dwells at the gateway to the sea"** — Ellicott explains the Hebrew is plural: "the approaches to the sea" or harbours. Tyre had two harbours, both remarkably good: the "Egyptian" facing south and the "Sidonian" facing north. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Block, notes the verb *yashab* ("to sit/dwell") here "speaks of occupying with authority, that is, ruling." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

---

### vv. 4–7: The Ship's Construction

**v. 4:** "Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders perfected your beauty." — Gill: Tyre's borders were "fixed by the Lord himself" in the midst of the seas, standing half a mile from the continent until Alexander made it a peninsula. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm) The Expositor's Bible notes that the ship image was "probably suggested to Ezekiel by the picturesque situation of Tyre on her sea-girt rock." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 5:** "Cypress from Senir … cedar from Lebanon to make a mast." — Ellicott: Senir was the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9). The timber was likely cypress, esteemed for shipbuilding because of "its lightness, durability, and freedom from the attacks of worms." The cedar mast: "Attaining a height of 290 ft. or more, cedars provided appropriate raw material for the mast" (Block, cited by Guzik). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 6:** "Oaks from Bashan … oars … coasts of Cyprus … deck, inlaid with ivory." — Ellicott notes the Hebrew for "benches" is better understood as the deck planking, inlaid with ivory in box-wood (reading the Hebrew words joined together as "in box-wood"). Chittim = Cyprus. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Gill, citing Jarchi, suggests the deck was made of box trees covered or inlaid with ivory, brought from Cyprus. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 7:** "Embroidered fine linen from Egypt … sail … blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah … awning." — Ellicott explains that state ships of antiquity were fitted with fine embroidered linen sails, the sail serving as "a sign" or pennon. Elishah = coasts of Asia Minor where the murex shellfish (source of purple dye) was abundant. The "awning" covered the ship's deck. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik adds: "Fundamentally, *nes* denotes a standard or flag … this sail served as a symbol of Tyrian self-assurance and pride." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

---

### vv. 8–9: The Crew

**v. 8:** "Sidon and Arvad were your oarsmen … your wise men … were your captains." — Ellicott: Sidon and Arvad (Greek Aradus, a rocky island north of Tripoli) furnished oarsmen; Tyre itself supplied the superior captains and pilots. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik notes that "a large Phoenician ship would have as many as 50 oarsmen in a crew of 200" (Wiersbe), and that these were biremes with two rows of oarsmen. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 9:** "Elders of Gebal were aboard as shipwrights, repairing your leaks." — Ellicott: Gebal = ancient Byblos (modern Gébeil), a famous Phoenician town whose people were renowned builders (employed by Solomon, 1 Kings 5:18 margin). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) The picture is that the whole widely-dispersed Phoenician race served Tyre.

---

### vv. 10–11: The Army / Defence

**v. 10:** "Men of Persia, Lydia, and Put served as warriors in your army." — Ellicott explains Tyre, like most commercial nations, depended on mercenaries. Persia (Elam) was just rising; Lud = Lydians (Hamite, from Mizraim); Phut = African tribe. Both Lud and Phut are repeatedly mentioned on Egyptian monuments as mercenary suppliers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 11:** "Men of Arvad and Helech … men of Gammad were in your towers." — Ellicott says "Gammadims" (only here in Scripture) is "probably not a proper name, but should be translated *brave men*." It is extremely unlikely that foreign troops would be entrusted with watchtower posts. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Gill notes various interpretations: some said dwarfs/pygmies (Vulgate), others "ambidexters" or left-handed men, but the most likely is inhabitants of a Phoenician place name. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Feinberg: "The valorous men (literally, *gammadim*) were perhaps from northern Syria." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**"They perfected your beauty"** — The refrain from v. 4 is repeated. Guzik: "The combination of it all was overwhelming. The city-kingdom of Tyre was like a mighty, beautiful, well-run ship." This makes the shipwreck of v. 26 all the more disastrous. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

---

### vv. 12–25: Tyre's Trade Empire

The Expositor's Bible explains that in this section "the city, although personified, is regarded as the emporium of the world's commerce, to which all the nations stream with their produce." The various commodities represent the cargo with which the ship is laden. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 12:** "Tarshish … silver, iron, tin, and lead." — Ellicott: Tarshish = Tartessus in Spain, famous for these metals, especially silver. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik also notes Tarshish was Jonah's intended destination (Jonah 1:3). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 13:** "Javan, Tubal, and Meshech … slaves and bronze utensils." — Ellicott: Javan = Ionia/Greece; Tubal and Meshech = Tibareni and Moschi between the Black and Caspian Seas, famous for slaves and copper. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

On the slave trade, Guzik notes: "This treatment of human beings like property and mere tools for economic profit was contrary to God's law and the dignity of all humanity created in His image." Amos had already rebuked Tyre for slave trafficking (Amos 1:9-10). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 14:** "Beth-togarmah … horses, war horses, and mules." — Ellicott: Togarmah = Armenia, dealing in horses and asses from most ancient times (Genesis 10:3). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 15:** "Dedan … ivory tusks and ebony." — Ellicott distinguishes two Dedans: this one is Hamitic, descended from Cush (Genesis 10:7), located in Arabia on the Persian Gulf. "Horns of ivory" is literally "horns of teeth" — a commercial term from the shape of elephant tusks. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 16:** "Aram … turquoise, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies." — Ellicott notes "emeralds" is now understood as carbuncle; the word for "fine linen" here is a different Phoenician word probably meaning cotton from Babylon. "Agate" (margin: chrysoprase) is probably the ruby. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 17:** "Judah and the land of Israel … wheat from Minnith, cakes and honey, oil and balm." — Ellicott: Minnith was in Ammon (Judges 11:33), rich in wheat; Tyre obtained its products through Israelite middlemen. The word "Pannag" (KJV) is uncertain — may be a sweet confection like grape syrup. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Clarke: "The Jews traded with the Tyrians in wheat, stacte, balsam, honey, oil, and resin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 18:** "Damascus … wine from Helbon, wool from Zahar." — Ellicott identifies Helbon as a village north of Damascus, still devoted to vine-growing, producing the costliest wine (probably the wine of Chalybon prized in Persia). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 19:** "Casks of wine from Izal … wrought iron, cassia, and sweet cane." — Ellicott argues that "Dan also and Javan" (KJV) is probably a misreading: the conjunction "and" should be part of the name *Vedan* (perhaps Aden), and Javan here is not Greece but an Arabian place (Yemen). "Going to and fro" (KJV) = from Uzal (ancient Sanaa, capital of Yemen), famous for sword blades ("bright iron") and spices. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 20:** "Dedan … saddlecloths for riding." — This is the Semitic Dedan (different from v. 15), also mentioned in Ezekiel 25:13 and Jeremiah 49:8. "Precious clothes for chariots" (KJV) = literally "clothes of spreading," meaning saddlecloths. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 21:** "Arabia and all the princes of Kedar … lambs, rams, and goats." — Ellicott: "Arabia" in the OT never means the whole peninsula, only the desert part of nomadic tribes. Kedar = Ishmaelite nomadic pastoral race (Genesis 25:13). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 22:** "Sheba and Raamah … gold, the finest of all spices, and precious stones." — Both Hamite tribes descended from Cush (Genesis 10:7), occupying southeast Arabia on the Bay of Oman. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Trapp: "Pliny reports of cinnamon that in his time a pound of it was worth a thousand denarii, that is, 150 crowns of our money." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 23:** "Haran, Canneh, and Eden … Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad." — Ellicott traces these to Mesopotamia: Haran = Charræ in NW Mesopotamia (junction of two great caravan routes); Canneh = Calneh (Genesis 10:10, later Ctesiphon); Eden = a town on the Euphrates. Sheba traded at Carrhæ. Asshur = Sura on the Euphrates, not Assyria. Chilmad = perhaps Charmande of Xenophon, "a great city beyond the Euphrates." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 24:** "Fine garments of blue, embroidered work, and multicolored rugs." — Ellicott renders "chests of rich apparel" as "treasures of twisted yarn," and "made of cedar" as "strong." An extensive yarn trade existed from Babylonia to Tyre. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

---

### vv. 25–28: The Shipwreck

**v. 25:** "The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea." — Ellicott says "ships of Tarshish" means ships of the largest size (like "East Indiaman"), not necessarily from Tarshish. The uncertain Hebrew word translated "did sing of thee" (KJV) is debated: probably "bulwarks" or "caravans" — "Thy great ships were at once thy defence and the means of thy commerce." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) The Expositor's Bible: at this point the various commodities represent the cargo with which the ship is laden; "Ships of Tarshish … wait upon her, and fill her with all sorts of precious things." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 26:** "Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea." — The key turning point. Ellicott notes the east wind is "powerful, gusty, and dangerous in the Levant," linking to Psalm 48:7: "Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Gill identifies the east wind as "Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldean army … because Babylon, from whence they came, lay somewhat to the east of Tyre." The Targum reads: "a king who is strong as the east wind hath broken thee." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik: "Even the best and strongest of ships is vulnerable to the power of the wind and the seas. Everything was fine for Tyre until it wasn't." He cites Morgan: "The Bible and history make one cause in their revelation of the peril of material prosperity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

The Expositor's Bible notes the image suggests two ideas: "one is that Tyre perished under the weight of her own commercial greatness, and the other that her ruin was hastened through the folly of her rulers. But the main idea is that the destruction of the city was wrought by the power of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 27:** "Your wealth, wares, and merchandise … will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall." — Ellicott: "The thought is that all that went to make up the strength and the glory of Tyre perished in one great catastrophe." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Gill: the sea broke in upon the city, washed all away, and left it a bare rock (see Ezekiel 26:4). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 28:** "The countryside will shake when your sailors cry out." — Ellicott: "suburbs" (KJV) means an open place around a building or city; as Tyre had no land around it, it is used in a general sense — "all thy surroundings." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

---

### vv. 29–36: The World Mourns

**v. 29:** "All who handle the oars will abandon their ships … stand on the shore." — Ellicott: the colonies and dependencies of Tyre are "the smaller craft which escape to the shore, and there lament the fall of their mistress." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Block: "Lesser vessels might be expected to perish in a Mediterranean squall, but surely not this proud monarch of the seas!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 30:** "They will raise their voices … cry out bitterly … throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes." — Ellicott notes "against thee" (KJV) is better "over thee" — the nations were not hostile but mourned over Tyre's engulfment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 31:** "They will shave their heads … wrap themselves in sackcloth." — Guzik, citing Feinberg: shaving bald was "a mourning custom which was connected with pagan superstitions and was forbidden in the Mosaic legislation (Deuteronomy 14:1)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 32:** "'Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?'" — Gill: the contrast is poignant — "she is not now Tyre the renowned, but Tyre the destroyed … she, in whom was heard the voice of joy and singing, is now mute." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm) The Expositor's Bible renders it poetically: "Who was like Tyre [so glorious] — In the midst of the sea?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 33:** "When your wares went out to sea, you satisfied many nations. You enriched the kings of the earth." — Gill: "thou filledst many people" — Tyre supplied everyone's needs fully; "thou didst enrich the kings of the earth" through tolls, customs, and by furnishing gold, silver, and precious stones. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

**v. 34:** "Now you are shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters." — The Expositor's Bible renders it: "Now art thou broken from the seas — In depths of the waters; Thy merchandise and all thy multitude — Are fallen therein." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html)

**v. 35:** "All the people of the coastlands are appalled … their kings shudder with fear; their faces are contorted." — The Expositor's Bible notes the prophet "drops the figure of the ship" and speaks plainly of the final overthrow. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html) Guzik, citing Taylor: "the terror on their faces is really selfish fear for the consequences that will come to them before long." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**v. 36:** "Those who trade among the nations hiss at you; you have come to a horrible end and will be no more." — Ellicott explains "hiss" is not mockery but "calling for" (as in Isaiah 5:26; Zechariah 10:8) — the people who had commercial connection with Tyre "shall call for her in vain." She shall be "a sudden destruction, and shall not be for ever." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm) Guzik, citing Clarke, says "shall shriek for thee" — "This powerfully expresses the sensation made on the feelings of the spectators on the shore when they saw the vessel swallowed up." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ

Because this chapter is predominantly a historical-commercial lament with a sustained metaphor, major doctrinal differences between Protestant traditions are minimal. Most interpreters read the chapter with remarkable agreement. However, a few nuances emerge:

**Reformed / Covenant Theology Emphasis:** The Expositor's Bible (Nicoll, 1887) emphasizes that "the real god of Tyre was not Baal nor Melkarth, but the king, or any other object that might serve as a symbol of her civic greatness." It frames Tyre's judgment as illustrating the spiritual danger of "the successful pursuit of the finite interests of human life" displacing thought of God — a classic Reformed emphasis on idolatry of the heart. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-27.html) Hengstenberg similarly emphasizes that the purpose is to demonstrate "the vanity of all worldly power" and "the indestructibleness of the kingdom of God," warning God's people against despondency when contemplating worldly glory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/ezekiel-27.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes practical application: "riches without God leave us spiritually empty and vulnerable … material success pursued in defiance of God's law — especially when built on the exploitation of others — cannot stand." He specifically highlights the slave trade (v. 13) as violating human dignity. He also connects Tyre typologically to Revelation 18 (the fall of Babylon), a common end-times application: "This great lamentation is an advance demonstration of what the whole world will do when Satan's system, 'Babylon the great,' collapses." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill's approach is heavily focused on historical-geographical identification and translation issues. He uniquely connects Tyre to "mystical Tyre" (Rome) in Revelation 17:1 and 18:7, reflecting a historic Baptist identification of Papal Rome with Babylon. He also offers a pastoral note rarely found in older commentaries: "it may teach us, that even wicked men are to be pitied, when in distress and calamity." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/27.htm)

**Evangelical Holiness / Devotional (Church Pulpit Commentary):** Draws a direct application to modern Britain: "Let our great mercantile nation, the Tyre of modern times, beware. She must rest her security, not on her navies or material resources … but on the favour of God and the righteousness which alone exalteth a nation." It also applies the shipwreck metaphor to individual souls: "How often it happens that individual souls … start in life richly dowered … but their career is one of bitter disappointment … their love of pleasure and the absence of self-control, bring them into great waters, where they become irretrievably broken. Only One can arrest that fate — He Who slept through the night-storm till the disciples awoke Him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/ezekiel-27.html)

**Baptist / Devotional (Kingcomments):** Emphasises the fatal lack: "the LORD is not on board. That is why it suffers shipwreck, despite all the solid and beautiful materials." It connects the spiritual lesson to 1 Timothy 1:19 about Christians suffering "shipwreck concerning their faith if they reject a good conscience." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-27.html)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):** No specific results were fetched. However, Ellicott and the Expositor's Bible, though older, employ critical scholarship regarding geography and text. Ellicott's extensive notes on the commercial geography of the ancient Near East reflect the best 19th-century scholarship, identifying places such as Tarshish (Tartessus, Spain), Javan (Ionia/Greece), Tubal and Meshech (between Black and Caspian Seas), and the distinction between the two Dedans (Hamitic vs. Semitic). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/27.htm)

**Catholic / Orthodox:** Pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org were not retrievable in this session.

**Popular Modern Teaching:** No prosperity-gospel or Word of Faith interpretations specific to Ezekiel 27 were found in the accessed sources. However, the chapter's warning about material prosperity could be seen as a direct challenge to any theology that equates wealth with divine favour. Guzik's comment is pointed: "riches without God are unable to satisfy the heart of man and often keep many from dependence upon God. Has not this spirit invaded the church, and does it not pervade the lives of too many Christians?" (Feinberg, cited by Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-27/)
